question: What are the eligibility requirements to get a study permit?
answer:
You can come to Canada to study if you 
- are enrolled at a DLI
- prove you have enough money to pay for
- your tuition fees
- living expenses for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada and
- return transportation for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada
- obey the law, have no criminal record and get a police certificate (if required)
- are in good health and get a medical exam (if required) and
- prove to an officer that you will leave Canada when your study permit expires

(Source: [2] Study permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/eligibility.html)

question: My study permit expired before I applied for my PGWP. What can I do?
answer:
If your study permit expired before you applied for your PGWP, you have two options: 

1. Apply for a visitor record to stay in Canada longer (Source: [1] Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html).

If you stay in Canada and let your permit expire, you must apply to restore your status as a student to apply for your PGWP (Source: [1] Post-graduation work permit: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/after-graduation/eligibility.html).

question: What is the difference between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit?
answer:
According to the sources, the main differences between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit are:

- An open work permit lets you work for any employer in Canada, except those who are on the non-compliant list or offer certain services (Source: [2] Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).
- An employer-specific work permit, on the other hand, requires a job offer and is tied to the specific employer and job (Source: [3] Work permit: Apply from inside Canada – Eligibility and requirements, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/permit-inside/eligibility.html).

Additionally, an open work permit does not require a labour market impact assessment or an offer of employment, and the employer does not need to pay the employer compliance fee (Source: [2] Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).

question: How long can my parents stay in Canada with a super visa?
answer:
If you entered Canada before June 22, 2023, your parents can stay in Canada for the length of time the border officer granted them when they entered Canada, which can be up to 2 years. They can either leave Canada before the end of their authorized stay and re-enter Canada, or apply to extend their stay in Canada and be approved for an extension of up to 2 years. The border officer may let them stay for 5 years if they still meet all the eligibility requirements for a super visa. (Source: [1] Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

If your parents entered Canada on or after June 22, 2023, they’re eligible to stay for 5 years at a time. (Source: [2] Super visa for parents and grandparents – How long you can stay in Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/parent-grandparent-super-visa/length-stay-canada.html)

question: Who is eligible to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada?
answer:
According to the sources, to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner, you must meet the requirements listed in [3] Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor and [5] Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor.

You must not be inadmissible to Canada and the relationship should be genuine, not only for the purpose of getting permanent resident status.

For a spouse:
- You must be legally married to them.
- They must be at least 18 years old.
- They can be any gender.
- They must not be inadmissible to Canada.

For a common-law partner:
- You must not be legally married to them.
- They must be at least 18 years old.
- They can be any gender.
- They must have lived with you for at least 12 consecutive months, meaning you've lived together continuously for 1 year in a conjugal relationship, without any long periods apart.
- Any time spent away from each other during the 12-month period should have been short and temporary.

(Source: [3] Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)
(Source: [5] Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)

question: How long do I need to have been physically present in Canada to apply for citizenship?

question: Who has to take the Canadian citizenship test?
answer:
According to the sources, most permanent residents will follow the regular application process for adults and children, but it's not explicitly stated who has to take the test. However, it's mentioned that if you fail the test, you'll have up to 3 chances to pass, and if you fail all 3 times, you'll be invited to a hearing with a citizenship official. 

It's also mentioned that if you belong to one of these groups, you may also be eligible for another application type: "Take the test" (Source: [1] Canadian citizenship, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship.html). 

However, the most direct information is in source [5] Citizenship test: Study for the test, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/study.html, which states that "Apply for citizenship as an adult or minor" is the process for most permanent residents, but it doesn't explicitly state who has to take the test.

question: What happens at the citizenship ceremony?
answer:
At the citizenship ceremony, you will:

- Arrive at the ceremony location and have your identity verified (Source: [2] Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)
- Take the oath of citizenship (Source: [2] Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)
- Receive your certificate (Source: [4] Host a citizenship ceremony: About the citizenship ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/take-part-citizenship/host-citizenship-ceremony/about.html)
- Sign the Oath or Affirmation of Citizenship form (Source: [2] Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)
- Receive information about the citizenship certificate (Source: [5] Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)

Note: The specific details may vary depending on whether the ceremony is in-person or virtual.
